description: We are six students from The American College of Greece (Deree) in Athens, tackling Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts. Our skills span IT, software and hardware solutions, cybersecurity, data management and design. We aim to build a secure, easy-to-use system that combines astronauts’ physical health data and alerts crews before small issues become serious. Our team is full, but we’d love to connect with mentors in space medicine and health data.
summary:
VITAL is a health-monitoring dashboard designed for astronauts on long missions. Normal ranges usually come from Earth population averages, but in space each body adapts differently, so VITAL asks: is this reading normal for this person?

Seven pre-flight days set each astronaut's own baseline for six vitals: resting heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, exercise and mood. Every new reading gets a clear status: Nominal , Watch or Call Ground. Alerts escalate from crew member to medical officer to commander while mood and personal notes stay private to their owner. A 3D body scan with a NASA hazard lens shows where to look. 

In our simulated demo, sleep and blood oxygen look normal on Earth ranges, yet VITAL flags a personal drift on day 145.

This matters because on Moon and Mars missions, help from Earth is slow. VITAL helps crews notice change early and act, using simulated data and facts sourced from NASA and CSA.
details:
VITAL: "Your normal, not Earth's normal"

Team ACG DSA · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

 

SUMMARY

 

VITAL is a health check-in dashboard for a crew on a long space mission, built within 48 hours. Normal ranges usually come from population averages on Earth. VITAL asks a different question: is this reading normal for this person? It learns each astronaut's own baseline from a week of pre-flight readings and compares every new reading with it.
This is a software-only entry. All readings are simulated, and every screen says so.

 

WHAT IT DOES

- Personal baseline. Seven pre-flight readings give each person a mean and spread for six indicators: resting heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, exercise and mood. A calibration wizard can simulate that week or take the astronaut's own readings.
- Two ways to catch change. A single reading at least two personal spreads from normal is Watch, and at least three is Call ground. Two trend detectors, EWMA (a smoothed trend line) and CUSUM (a running sum of small deviations), also catch slow drifts that no single reading shows.
- Status at a glance. Nominal ●, Watch ▲ or Call ground ■, always shown as a colour, a shape and a word, with a plain-language reason. Call ground is a prompt to contact ground, not a diagnosis.
- Daily check-in and quick log. The crew member confirms the simulated readings or types their own. A quick log saves a mood, any number of one-tap entries and a note together as one entry.
- Interactive body scan. A particle figure with skeleton, organs and blood vessels. Its regions glow by status, and the heart beats at the resting heart rate on screen. A Hazard Lens dims everything not linked to the NASA hazard you pick: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity, or closed and hostile environments.
- Same reading, four normals. One reading laid on each crew member's own normal. At 63 bpm the Flight Engineer is 1.7 spreads above their own normal, the Commander 3.4 above theirs and the Systems Officer 1.2 below. You can drag the value or pick another vital.
- Mission timeline. A simulated 1,095-day Mars mission (transit, Mars surface, return). A play button moves the mission day forward by itself, and the dashboard, charts and body scan follow. A thin line under the day label shows progress through the mission.
- A background that follows the person on screen. It is calm when that person is Nominal, rippling and amber on Watch, and taller and red-tinted on Call ground. Status is still carried by text, shape and colour; the background only sets the mood.
- Crew view and reports. The crew is sorted most urgent first, and each person has a daily report for ground to copy, save or print. The Chief Medical Officer gets one report for the whole crew and can send it to the Commander. An "I'm OK" button puts an acknowledgement on the record.
- Built for use under stress. Large touch targets, keyboard shortcuts, a command palette, voice commands (where the browser supports them), a red-shifted night mode, and a table view for every chart.
- Reviewable without us. A first-time visitor is offered a two-minute guided tour (Presenter mode, ten steps), and a link ending in ?tour opens straight into it. Every screen has Replay the tour and Reset demo links.

 

PRIVACY

Mood values, personal notes, personal reports and pre-flight calibration are visible only to the crew member who owns them. For mood, everyone else sees only a status level. The same holds inside the crew report: the copy built for the Commander leaves out the medical officer's notes too.

 

BUILT WITH

- Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Pydantic and Uvicorn, with exact pinned versions. The statistics are written in plain Python.
- Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber, ECharts, Tailwind CSS and Zustand.
- Testing: pytest, Vitest and Playwright, with browser tests at laptop, desktop and phone sizes.
- Run it: with Python 3.11+ and Node.js installed, one command (node start.mjs) installs, builds and starts everything on localhost. No database, no accounts, no internet once installed.
- Resilience: if the server can't be reached, check-ins and log entries are kept in the browser and sent when it answers.

 

DATA AND SCIENTIFIC HONESTY

- All crew readings are simulated. The crew carries our team's names, but none of the readings are ours. Every screen is labelled as simulated.
- Every health statement comes from three NASA Human Research Program pages (hazards, risks, ongoing research) and two Canadian Space Agency pages: 75 statements, each tied to a quoted sentence on its page. The app shows no sources, because it is a tool for the crew. The full list is in docs/SOURCES.txt in the repository.
- We wrote no medical thresholds. Everything is relative to the individual, and the comparison panel adds no verdicts of its own.
- The alert method is labelled provisional until medical experts review it. VITAL flags a change and tells the crew to call ground. It does not diagnose, and it makes no claim of NASA endorsement.
- Anything still waiting for a sourced fact is listed as planned.

 

INTENDED IMPACT

On Moon and Mars missions, crews will have to track their own health while help from Earth is slow and increasingly hard to reach. NASA notes that instructions and medical care become harder to receive the deeper astronauts travel. VITAL gives each person a clear summary of how they compare with themselves, so the crew can notice a change early and decide what to do.
Our own idea, not NASA's: the same personal-baseline approach could help people on Earth who are far from care, such as seafarers, remote workers and older people. The Canadian Space Agency says its spaceflight research can help people with balance problems, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disorders and Type-2 diabetes, and that astronauts' changes resemble accelerated ageing.

 

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- "Your own ruler." The baseline is the person, not a population, and one picture shows it: the same reading means different things for different people.
- A body scan that is the interface. Regions glow by status, the heart beats at the person's own pulse, and the Hazard Lens ties NASA's five hazards to the body.
- A timeline you can watch. Play the mission and see the drift appear.
- Two independent trend detectors in plain Python, explained to the crew in plain words.
- Reviewable without us. The guided tour, the ?tour link, saving that survives a lost connection, and one-command setup.

 

KNOWN LIMITS

The readings are simulated. State is kept in server memory, so a restart clears it. The method raises more false alarms than a real system could accept: in our quiet simulated scenario about one crew-day in five shows Watch and about one in 65 shows Call ground. That is why it is labelled provisional. The app needs its small server and is not an offline-only static page.

 

AI ASSISTANCE

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for coding, design, debugging and fact-checking, all final decisions were approved by the team.

 

With respect to NASA and humanity,
Serafeim Sinnis, Petros Kotsomitopoulos, Grigorios Kiousopoulos and Rafailia Falelaki
